blocks.text: The chapter names gates, towers, and stretches of wall as the two thanksgiving processions move around Jerusalem. Archaeology supports Persian-period occupation and administration in Jerusalem and Yehud, but it does not establish an uncontested route, height, or complete circuit for Nehemiah’s wall. Specific modern identifications of these features, including any proposed route for the processions, should therefore be treated as provisional.

The dedication of the wall belongs within a wider account in which Jerusalem is repopulated, two thanksgiving processions dedicate the wall, and provisions are organized to support priests and Levites. The book also combines vivid first-person material associated with Nehemiah with third-person narrative, lists, Ezra material, and editorial transitions. Its varied form resists reading the whole book as either a single autobiography or a wholly fictional narrative.
